l: chest, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: At the king's command a chest was made and set outside the gate of the LORD's house to receive the tax of Moses. The princes and people filled it, and the king's scribe and the chief priest's officer emptied it and returned it to its place day by day, gathering money in abundance.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Joash intended to restore the LORD's house, and after the Levites' delay the work was funded through the chest. Hired masons, carpenters, and metalworkers carried it forward, and the house was set up as designed and strengthened. The remaining money was made into vessels for ministering and offering, and the account of the rebuilding is said to be written in the commentary of the book of the kings.

l: killing of Zechariah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Conspirators stoned Zechariah in the court of the LORD's house at the commandment of King Joash, who did not remember the kindness of Zechariah's father Jehoiada. Zechariah asked the LORD to look at it and repay it, and the text then describes the Syrian defeat and Joash's murder by his servants, which came for the blood of Jehoiada's sons.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Amaziah begins his twenty-nine-year reign over Judah, doing right but not with a perfect heart, and executes his father's killers while sparing their children according to the law of Moses. He musters 300,000 men of Judah and Benjamin and hires 100,000 men from Israel, but dismisses the Israelites at a man of God's warning, which enrages them. He defeats ten thousand of Seir's children in the Valley of Salt, yet then brings home and worships the gods of Seir, ignoring a prophet's rebuke. He challenges Joash king of Israel, rejects Joash's warning, and is defeated at Beth Shemesh; Joash breaks down part of Jerusalem's wall and plunders the temple and palace. Amaziah later flees a conspiracy to Lachish, where he is killed, and he is buried in the City of Judah.

l: Amaziah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Amaziah became king of Judah at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years, doing right but not with a perfect heart. He defeated Seir's children, then worshiped their gods, ignored a prophet, challenged Joash of Israel, and was defeated and taken to Jerusalem. He later fled a conspiracy to Lachish and was killed there.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The LORD is said to command that fathers and children not die for each other's sins, and he is not with Israel or the children of Ephraim. His anger burned against Amaziah for worshiping Seir's gods, and he sent a prophet and determined to destroy him. The defeat by Israel was of God because Judah sought the gods of Edom.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Jerusalem is where Amaziah reigned and where his mother Jehoaddan was from. Joash broke down its wall from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits, and took its treasures. A conspiracy against Amaziah was made there.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Judah, with Benjamin, supplied 300,000 chosen men for Amaziah's army and threw ten thousand captives from the top of a rock. Its cities were raided by the dismissed Israelite soldiers from Samaria to Beth Horon, killing three thousand. Judah was defeated by Israel at Beth Shemesh and its men fled to their tents.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Israel supplied 100,000 mighty men hired by Amaziah for one hundred talents of silver, but they were sent home on a man of God's warning. In anger they raided Judah's cities. King Joash of Israel later defeated Judah, broke Jerusalem's wall, and took plunder and hostages to Samaria.

l: Seir, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The children of Seir were struck down, ten thousand of them, by Amaziah in the Valley of Salt. Ten thousand more were taken alive by Judah and thrown from the top of a rock, so that all were broken in pieces. Amaziah afterward took their gods home.

l: gods of Seir, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Amaziah brought the gods of the children of Seir home, set them up as his own, bowed to them, and burned incense to them. A prophet asked why he sought gods that had not delivered their own people from his hand. This idolatry provoked the LORD's anger.

l: Joash king of Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, answered Amaziah's challenge with a parable of a thistle and a cedar, telling him to stay home. He then defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh, captured Amaziah, broke down part of Jerusalem's wall, and took gold, silver, vessels, treasures, and hostages to Samaria. Amaziah outlived him by fifteen years.

l: Beth Shemesh, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Beth Shemesh, a place belonging to Judah, is where Joash and Amaziah met face to face. Judah was defeated there, and Joash took Amaziah captive at that place.

l: battle of Beth Shemesh, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Amaziah's challenge led Joash of Israel to go up and meet him at Beth Shemesh. Judah was defeated by Israel and every man fled to his tent. The text says this was of God, so that Judah would be delivered to enemies for seeking Edom's gods.

l: Lachish, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Lachish is where Amaziah fled when the conspiracy against him arose in Jerusalem. His pursuers sent after him there and killed him.

l: Amaziah's death by conspiracy, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy was made against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, where the conspirators sent after him and killed him. His body was brought back on horses and buried with his fathers in the City of Judah.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Uzziah, sixteen years old, is made king by the people of Judah in place of his father Amaziah and reigns fifty-two years in Jerusalem. He does right in the LORD's eyes, seeks God in the days of Zechariah, and prospers: he defeats the Philistines and others, receives tribute from the Ammonites, builds towers and cisterns, farms, and equips a large army with weapons and siege devices. Once strong, his heart is lifted up and he enters the LORD's temple to burn incense on the altar of incense. Azariah the priest and eighty priests resist him, saying only the consecrated sons of Aaron may burn incense, and Uzziah's anger is met by leprosy breaking out on his forehead. He lives as a leper in a separate house until his death while his son Jotham judges the people, and he is buried with his fathers in the kings' burial field, with Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, having written his acts.

l: Uzziah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Uzziah is made king at sixteen by the people of Judah in place of his father Amaziah, reigns fifty-two years, and prospers while he seeks God, becoming strong through military victories, fortifications, farming and a large equipped army. When strong, his heart is lifted up and he enters the temple to burn incense, becomes angry at the priests' rebuke, and is struck with leprosy. He lives in a separate house, cut off from the LORD's house, until his death, and is buried with his fathers in the kings' burial field, with Jotham reigning in his place.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: The LORD makes Uzziah prosper as long as he seeks Him, and God helps him against the Philistines, Arabians and Meunim. After Uzziah trespasses in the temple, the LORD strikes him with leprosy, which cuts him off from the LORD's house.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: The LORD's temple contains the altar of incense, which Uzziah enters to burn incense. Within it, beside the altar, leprosy breaks out on his forehead before the priests, who thrust him out, and afterwards he is cut off from the LORD's house.

l: Azariah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Azariah the priest, called the chief priest, goes into the temple after Uzziah with eighty priests. He and the priests resist the king, tell him that burning incense belongs to the consecrated sons of Aaron, and thrust him out when they see he is leprous.

l: priests (the eighty priests with Azariah), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Eighty valiant priests of the LORD go in after Uzziah with Azariah and resist him, saying he has trespassed and must leave the sanctuary. They see the leprosy on his forehead and quickly thrust him out of the temple.

l: leprosy, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Leprosy breaks out on Uzziah's forehead while he is angry with the priests, holding a censer beside the altar of incense. It is described as a strike from the LORD, and it leaves him a leper until his death, living in a separate house and buried apart in the kings' field because "He is a leper."

l: Uzziah's trespass in the temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: After becoming strong, Uzziah's heart is lifted up, and he acts corruptly by entering the LORD's temple to burn incense on the altar of incense. The priests tell him this is not for him but for the consecrated sons of Aaron, and his persistence in anger is followed by leprosy, ending his role in the LORD's house.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Chapter 27 describes the reign of Jotham, who became king of Judah at twenty-five and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem; his mother was Jerushah daughter of Zadok. He did right in the LORD's eyes like his father Uzziah, though he did not enter the temple and the people still acted corruptly. He built the upper gate of the LORD's house, worked on the wall of Ophel, and built cities, fortresses and towers in Judah. He fought the king of the children of Ammon and prevailed, receiving silver, wheat and barley as tribute for three years. After he died he was buried in David's city and his son Ahaz succeeded him.

l: Jotham, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Jotham began to reign at twenty-five and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Jerushah daughter of Zadok. He did right in the LORD's eyes as his father Uzziah had, built the upper gate of the LORD's house, the wall of Ophel, and cities, fortresses and towers in Judah, and defeated the king of the children of Ammon. He became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God, and he was buried in David's city.

l: Ahaz, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Ahaz is named as Jotham's son. He reigned in his father's place after Jotham died and was buried in David's city.

l: children of Ammon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: The king of the children of Ammon fought with Jotham and was prevailed against. The children of Ammon then gave Jotham one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat and ten thousand cors of barley in that year, and the same amount in the second and third years.

l: Jotham's reign, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Jotham's reign lasted sixteen years in Jerusalem, beginning when he was twenty-five. It was marked by right conduct in the LORD's eyes, building projects on the temple's upper gate, the Ophel wall, and cities, fortresses and towers in Judah, though the people still acted corruptly. The rest of his acts and wars are said to be written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, and it ended with his death and Ahaz's accession.

l: war with Ammon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Jotham fought the king of the children of Ammon and prevailed against them. As a result the Ammonites paid a yearly tribute of one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat and ten thousand cors of barley for three years.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Chapter 28 describes the sixteen-year reign of Ahaz over Judah, who did evil by making images for the Baals, burning his children in the fire, and sacrificing at high places. As a result, the LORD delivered him to the king of Syria and to the king of Israel, whose commander Pekah killed 120,000 men of Judah in one day, and Israel took 200,000 captives to Samaria. The prophet Oded, backed by several Ephraimite leaders, persuaded the army to release the captives, who were clothed, fed, and returned to Jericho. Ahaz then appealed to the king of Assyria while Edomites and Philistines attacked Judah, but Tilgath-pilneser troubled him rather than helping him. Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, cut up the vessels of God's house, shut the LORD's house, and set up altars and high places everywhere, and when he died he was buried in Jerusalem but not in the tombs of the kings, with Hezekiah reigning after him.

l: Ahaz, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Ahaz began to reign at twenty and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, doing evil by following the kings of Israel, making molten images for the Baals, burning his children in the fire, and sacrificing at high places. He sought help from Assyria by giving it treasure from the LORD's house and the royal houses, but it did not help him. He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, cut up the vessels of God's house, shut its doors, and built altars and high places throughout Judah. He died, was buried in Jerusalem but not in the kings' tombs, and was succeeded by his son Hezekiah.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: The LORD delivered Ahaz and Judah into the hands of the king of Syria and the king of Israel because of their unfaithfulness, and brought Judah low because Ahaz acted without restraint. His anger against Judah, and fierce wrath against Israel for its own guilt, are stated by Oded and the Ephraimite leaders. He is provoked to anger by Ahaz's high places and altars to other gods.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Judah suffered under Ahaz, being struck by Syria and Israel, losing 120,000 valiant men in one day, and having many taken captive. It was also raided by Edomites and Philistines, who took cities of the lowland and the South and lived in them. Ahaz made high places in every city of Judah for other gods.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Israel, as the northern kingdom, struck Ahaz with great slaughter and carried 200,000 women, sons, and daughters captive to Samaria with much plunder. After Oded's rebuke and the Ephraimite leaders' warning that its guilt was already great, its armed men released the captives and the plunder. Ahaz is also said to have walked in the ways of the kings of Israel.

l: gods of Damascus, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, reasoning that they had helped the kings of Syria who defeated him. The text says they instead became the ruin of him and of all Israel.

l: Pekah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah in one day. The text attributes this to Judah having forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.

l: captives of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: About 200,000 women, sons, and daughters of Judah were carried off to Samaria by Israel, along with plunder. After Oded's intervention, named Ephraimite men clothed, shod, fed, anointed them, carried the feeble on donkeys, and brought them to their brothers at Jericho, the city of palm trees.

l: Oded, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Oded, a prophet of the LORD in Samaria, went out to meet the returning army and told them that Judah's defeat came from the LORD's anger and that their own rage had reached heaven. He told them to send back the captives from their brothers, warning of the LORD's fierce wrath. The armed men then left the captives and plunder.

l: Tilgath-pilneser, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came to Ahaz after Ahaz sent for help, but he gave him trouble and did not strengthen him. Ahaz had paid him with treasure from the LORD's house and the royal houses without benefit.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: Hezekiah, a 25-year-old king of Judah who does right in the LORD's eyes, opens and repairs the doors of the LORD's house in the first month of his first year. He summons the priests and Levites, tells them to sanctify themselves and remove filthiness from the temple, and explains that the fathers' unfaithfulness brought the LORD's wrath. Named Levites and their brothers cleanse the house in sixteen days and report that the altar, the table of show bread, and the vessels Ahaz threw away are prepared. Hezekiah then gathers the city's princes and offers seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, sanctuary, and Judah, with music according to David's commandment. The assembly brings sacrifices, thank offerings, and burnt offerings, the Levites help skin them because the priests are too few, and Hezekiah and the people rejoice that the service of the house was set in order.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: Hezekiah begins to reign at twenty-five, reigns twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, and does right in the LORD's eyes like David his father. In his first year he opens and repairs the temple doors, commands the priests and Levites to cleanse the house, and plans to make a covenant with the LORD. He leads the sin offering, commands the burnt offering and the singing, invites the assembly to bring offerings, and rejoices with the people when the service is set in order.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The LORD is described as the God of the fathers whose wrath fell on Judah and Jerusalem because the fathers were unfaithful, leaving them to the sword and captivity. He has chosen the Levites to stand before him, minister, and burn incense. His commandment through David, Gad the seer, and Nathan the prophet governed the temple music, and the people rejoice at what God had prepared for them, done suddenly.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The Levites are told by Hezekiah to sanctify themselves and carry the filthiness out of the holy place. Named men from the Kohathites, Merari, Gershonites, and the sons of Elizaphan, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun arise, gather their brothers, and cleanse the house, carrying the uncleanness to the brook Kidron. They play David's instruments, sing praises, and help skin the burnt offerings, being more upright in heart than the priests in sanctifying themselves.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The priests go into the inner part of the temple to cleanse it and bring the uncleanness out to the court. Sons of Aaron kill the bulls, rams, lambs, and male goats, sprinkle the blood on the altar, and make the sin offering for all Israel, while sounding trumpets. They are too few to skin all the burnt offerings, so the Levites help them until the priests have sanctified themselves.

l: temple (the LORD's house), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The temple had been neglected: its porch doors were shut, lamps put out, and no incense or burnt offerings made, and King Ahaz had thrown away its vessels. Hezekiah opens and repairs its doors, and it is cleansed and sanctified in eight days for the house itself after eight days for the porch. Afterward worship, sacrifice, and song fill it, and its service is set in order.

l: temple cleansing, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The cleansing begins on the first day of the first month, reaches the LORD's porch on the eighth day, and is finished on the sixteenth day. Priests bring out the uncleanness from the inner house to the court, and Levites carry it to the brook Kidron. The workers report to Hezekiah that the house, the altar of burnt offering, the table of show bread, and all vessels, including those Ahaz threw away, are cleansed and prepared.

l: sin offering, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: Seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats are brought as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. The priests sprinkle the blood of the bulls, rams, and lambs on the altar, and the male goats are brought before the king and assembly, who lay their hands on them. The priests kill the goats and make atonement with their blood for all Israel, at the king's command.

l: burnt offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: Hezekiah commands that the burnt offering be offered on the altar, and when it begins the LORD's song and the trumpets and David's instruments start and continue until it is finished. The assembly then brings seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs as burnt offerings, along with consecrated things of six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep. The offerings are abundant, accompanied by fat of the peace offerings and drink offerings, and the Levites help skin them.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: King Hezekiah sends letters and couriers throughout Israel and Judah, from Beersheba to Dan, inviting people to Jerusalem to keep the Passover in the second month because the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient number earlier. Many in Ephraim and Manasseh ridicule the couriers, but some men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humble themselves and come, and God gives Judah one heart to obey. A very great assembly removes the altars in Jerusalem, kills the Passover on the fourteenth day, and keeps the feast of unleavened bread, with Hezekiah praying for the unclean who ate otherwise than prescribed, and the LORD healing the people. The assembly joyfully keeps seven more days, supported by large gifts of bulls and sheep from Hezekiah and the princes. The priests bless the people and their prayer reaches heaven, and the joy is unmatched in Jerusalem since Solomon.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: Hezekiah sent letters to all Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, calling them to keep the Passover in Jerusalem in the second month after taking counsel with his princes and the assembly. He prayed for the unclean who sought God, spoke encouragingly to the Levites, and gave one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for offerings, and the LORD listened to him.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The LORD is described as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, gracious and merciful, who will not turn his face from those who return to him. He gave Judah one heart, listened to Hezekiah's prayer and healed the people, and heard the priests' blessing in his holy habitation in heaven.

l: Passover, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The Passover was kept in the second month because the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient number and the people had not gathered at the proper time. It was killed on the fourteenth day, with the Levites killing it for those who were not clean, and many ate it otherwise than as written until Hezekiah's prayer was answered.

l: feast of unleavened bread, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: A very great assembly kept the feast of unleavened bread in Jerusalem in the second month for seven days with great gladness, with the Levites and priests praising the LORD daily. The assembly then took counsel and kept another seven days with gladness.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: Israel was invited from Beersheba to Dan to return to the LORD and keep the Passover, with the warning not to be like their fathers who were given up to desolation. Many in Ephraim and Manasseh mocked the couriers, but some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came, and people from Israel took part in the rejoicing.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The hand of God came on Judah to give them one heart to carry out the commandment of the king and princes by the LORD's word. The assembly of Judah rejoiced together with the priests, Levites, those from Israel, and the foreigners living in Judah.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: Jerusalem was the place where the people were called to keep the Passover at the LORD's house, and where a great assembly gathered. The altars there were removed and thrown into the brook Kidron, and there had been no joy like this in Jerusalem since the time of Solomon.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient number at the usual time, and in the second month they were ashamed and sanctified themselves and brought burnt offerings into the LORD's house. They stood in their order, sprinkled the blood received from the Levites, praised the LORD, and finally blessed the people, with their prayer coming up to heaven.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The Levites were ashamed, sanctified themselves, and stood in their place according to the law of Moses. They killed the Passovers for everyone who was not clean, handed blood to the priests, praised the LORD with loud instruments, and were encouraged by Hezekiah for their good understanding in the LORD's service.

l: assembly (at Jerusalem), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 30
s: The assembly agreed with Hezekiah to keep the Passover in the second month, and a very great assembly gathered, removing the altars from Jerusalem. They kept the feast seven days, took counsel to keep seven more, received gifts of bulls and sheep from Hezekiah and the princes, and rejoiced greatly.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: After the Passover and related events, all Israel who were present went through Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh destroying pillars, Asherah poles, high places and altars, then returned to their own cities. King Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites into divisions for offerings and service, and provided the king's own portion for the regular and festival burnt offerings. He commanded the people in Jerusalem to give the priests' and Levites' portion, and the people responded with abundant first fruits and tithes, laid in heaps from the third to the seventh month. Azariah the chief priest told Hezekiah that there was plenty left over because the LORD had blessed his people, so Hezekiah had storerooms prepared, and Conaniah, Shimei, Kore and others were appointed to oversee and distribute the goods. The chapter concludes that Hezekiah did what was good, right and faithful, and prospered in all he did to seek his God.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and Levites, provided the king's portion for the burnt offerings, and commanded the people of Jerusalem to give the portion due to the priests and Levites. He blessed the LORD and Israel on seeing the heaps, questioned the priests about them, ordered rooms prepared in the LORD's house, and appointed overseers. He is described as doing what was good, right and faithful, and as prospering because he sought God with all his heart.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: All Israel who were present went out to Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh and destroyed the idolatrous objects, then returned to their possessions and cities. The children of Israel gave first fruits and tithes in abundance in response to Hezekiah's command.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: The LORD's law is the basis for the appointed offerings and for the priests' and Levites' devotion. Azariah says the LORD has blessed his people, which explains the plentiful store. Hezekiah acts faithfully before the LORD his God.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: The priests were organized by Hezekiah into divisions according to their service for burnt and peace offerings. Their portion was provided by the people so they could devote themselves to the LORD's law, and they were supplied through listings by genealogy and by named men in their cities. They ate and had enough, with much left over.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: The Levites were appointed by divisions for service, thanksgiving and praise in the gates of the LORD's camp, and were supported by the people's portion. Conaniah, Shimei, Kore and the overseers under them were Levites who managed the stored offerings, and Levites twenty years old and upward were listed by genealogy for their offices.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: The cities of Judah were where the pillars, Asherah poles, high places and altars were broken down. People of Israel and Judah living in Judah's cities brought tithes of cattle, sheep and dedicated things. Hezekiah's faithful practice is said to extend throughout all Judah.

l: Azariah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: Azariah, the chief priest of the house of Zadok, answered Hezekiah's question about the heaps. He said that since offerings began to be brought, they had eaten and had plenty left over because the LORD had blessed his people. He is also called the ruler of God's house, and took part in appointing the overseers.

l: Conaniah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: Conaniah the Levite was made ruler over the offerings, tithes and dedicated things brought into the prepared rooms, with his brother Shimei second. Ten named overseers served under him, appointed by Hezekiah and Azariah.

l: tithes and first fruits (offerings), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: After Hezekiah's command, the people gave first fruits of grain, new wine, oil, honey and all the field's increase, along with tithes of all things, cattle, sheep and dedicated things. These were brought in abundance and faithfully, and were stored and distributed to support the priests and Levites.

l: heaps (of offerings), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 31
s: The offerings were laid in heaps, begun in the third month and finished in the seventh month. Hezekiah and the princes blessed the LORD and Israel on seeing them, and Azariah explained that the heaps were the surplus left after the priests had eaten their fill. Rooms were then prepared in the LORD's house to store them.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Sennacherib king of Assyria invades Judah and threatens Jerusalem, so Hezekiah stops the springs, strengthens the wall, arms the people, and encourages them to trust that the LORD is with them. Sennacherib's servants mock Hezekiah and the LORD with speeches and letters, comparing the LORD to the powerless gods of other nations. Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah pray, and the LORD sends an angel who cuts off the Assyrian leaders, so Sennacherib returns home in shame and is killed by his own sons in his god's house. Afterward Hezekiah is exalted and grows rich, but pride after his illness and healing brings wrath that he and Jerusalem avert by humbling themselves, and God tests him regarding the Babylonian ambassadors. Hezekiah dies and is buried with honor, and Manasseh his son reigns in his place.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Hezekiah prepares Jerusalem against Sennacherib by stopping the springs, repairing the wall, strengthening Millo, making weapons, setting captains, and encouraging the people, and with Isaiah he prays and cries to heaven. After being delivered he is exalted, becomes very wealthy, falls ill and is given a sign, but becomes proud and brings wrath, then humbles himself; God tests him over the Babylonian ambassadors. He dies and is buried with honor, and Manasseh succeeds him.

l: Sennacherib, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, enters Judah, encamps against the fortified cities, and attacks Lachish while sending servants and letters to mock Hezekiah and the LORD. After the LORD's angel destroys his mighty men and captains, he returns in shame to his own land and is killed by the sword by those of his own body in the house of his god.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Judah is invaded by Sennacherib, who encamps against its fortified cities. Its people rest on Hezekiah's words, are saved by the LORD, and later come under wrath for Hezekiah's pride, which is averted when he humbles himself. Judah and Jerusalem honor Hezekiah at his death.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Jerusalem is threatened by Sennacherib, and its people on the wall are shouted at in the Jews' language to frighten them. Hezekiah fortifies it and the LORD saves its inhabitants from Sennacherib and all others. Many then bring gifts to the LORD at Jerusalem, and its inhabitants humble themselves along with Hezekiah.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: The LORD is declared by Hezekiah to be with the people to help and fight their battles, and is mocked by Sennacherib as no better than the gods of other nations. He answers the prayers of Hezekiah and Isaiah by sending an angel that cuts off the Assyrian leaders, and he saves Jerusalem. He also gives Hezekiah a sign in his illness, sends wrath over his pride, relents when he humbles himself, and tests him regarding the Babylonian ambassadors.

l: Assyrian siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 32
s: Sennacherib's forces invade Judah and threaten Jerusalem while he attacks Lachish, and his servants taunt the people and deliver letters insulting the LORD. Hezekiah's preparations include stopping the springs and strengthening the wall. The threat ends when the LORD's angel destroys the Assyrian mighty men, leaders, and captains, and Sennacherib withdraws in shame.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Chapter 33 recounts how Manasseh became king of Judah at twelve and reigned fifty-five years, rebuilding high places, raising altars to Baals and the army of the sky in the LORD's house, setting up an engraved idol there, sacrificing his children, and practicing sorcery. The LORD spoke to him and his people, but they did not listen, so Assyrian captains took Manasseh in chains to Babylon. In distress he humbled himself and prayed, and the LORD restored him to Jerusalem, after which he built an outer wall, placed captains in fortified cities, removed the foreign gods and idol, rebuilt the LORD's altar, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD, though the people still sacrificed at the high places. After Manasseh's death his son Amon reigned two years, did evil and did not humble himself, and was killed by his servants. The people of the land then executed the conspirators and made Josiah, Amon's son, king.

l: Manasseh, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Manasseh became king at twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, doing great evil by rebuilding high places, building altars to Baals and the army of the sky, placing an idol in God's house, passing his children through fire, and practicing sorcery. Taken in chains to Babylon by Assyrian captains, he humbled himself and prayed, was restored to Jerusalem, fortified the city and Judah, removed the foreign gods and idol, restored the LORD's altar, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD. He slept with his fathers, was buried in his own house, and was succeeded by his son Amon.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, who did not listen, and then brought the Assyrian captains against them. When Manasseh humbled himself and prayed, the LORD was entreated, heard his supplication, and returned him to Jerusalem, so that Manasseh knew the LORD was God. The LORD had said His name would be in Jerusalem forever and that Israel would not be removed from the land if they kept the law given by Moses.

l: Amon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Amon, Manasseh's son, began to reign at twenty-two and reigned two years in Jerusalem. He did evil as his father had, sacrificed to and served the engraved images Manasseh had made, and did not humble himself but trespassed more and more. His servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house, and Josiah his son was made king in his place.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were seduced by Manasseh into doing more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed. After Manasseh's repentance he commanded Judah to serve the LORD, and he put valiant captains in its fortified cities, though the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD. After Amon's death the people of the land killed the conspirators and made Josiah king.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Jerusalem was where Manasseh and later Amon reigned, and the place where the LORD had said His name would remain forever. Manasseh was returned there from Babylon and built an outer wall for David's city west of Gihon, running to the fish gate and around Ophel, raising it very high. He also cast the foreign altars out of the city.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Manasseh built altars in the LORD's house, including for all the army of the sky in its two courts, and set an engraved idol in God's house, where God had said He would put His name forever. After his restoration, Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house and the altars from the mountain of the house.

l: high places, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Manasseh rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down. Even after Manasseh's repentance and reforms, the people still sacrificed in the high places, but only to the LORD their God. The high places he built before humbling himself are recorded in the history of Hozai.

l: idol (Manasseh's engraved image), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Manasseh made an engraved image of an idol and set it in God's house, the place where God had said He would put His name forever. After he humbled himself, he took the idol out of the LORD's house and cast it out of the city. Amon later sacrificed to the engraved images Manasseh had made.

l: altars, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Manasseh raised altars for the Baals and built altars for the army of the sky in the LORD's house and its two courts. After his restoration he removed all the altars he had built in the mountain of the LORD's house and in Jerusalem and cast them out of the city. He then rebuilt the LORD's altar and offered peace offerings and thanksgiving sacrifices on it.

l: Manasseh’s captivity and repentance, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 33
s: Because Manasseh and his people did not listen to the LORD, Assyrian captains took him in chains and fetters to Babylon. In distress he begged the LORD and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and the LORD heard his supplication and brought him back to Jerusalem to his kingdom. His prayer, and how God listened to it, are said to be written in the acts of the kings of Israel and the history of Hozai.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Chapter 34 describes Josiah, who became king of Judah at age eight and began seeking God in his eighth year, then purged Judah, Jerusalem, and the lands of Israel of high places, Asherah poles, and images in his twelfth year. In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah to repair the house of the LORD, where Hilkiah the priest found the book of the law given by Moses. Shaphan read it to Josiah, who tore his clothes and sent Hilkiah and others to inquire of the prophetess Huldah. Huldah declared that the LORD would bring the written curses on the place, but that Josiah, because he humbled himself and wept, would be gathered to his grave in peace without seeing the evil. Josiah then gathered the people, read them the book of the covenant, and made a covenant before the LORD, and the people did not depart from the LORD all his days.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Josiah became king at age eight, reigned thirty-one years, did what was right in the LORD's eyes, and began seeking God in his eighth year. He purged idolatry, ordered the temple repaired, tore his clothes on hearing the law, and led the people in a covenant. He was told by Huldah that he would die in peace because of his humility.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: The LORD, through Huldah, declared that he would bring on the place and its inhabitants the curses written in the book because they had forsaken him and burned incense to other gods. He said he had heard Josiah's humility and would gather him to his grave in peace. His wrath is described as poured out and unquenched.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Judah was purged of high places, Asherah poles, and images by Josiah. Its people, with those of Jerusalem, were gathered to hear the book of the covenant, and the LORD declared the curses would come on the place. All his days they did not depart from following the LORD.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Jerusalem was purged of idolatry in Josiah's twelfth year, and Josiah returned there after destroying altars throughout Israel. Its inhabitants, including the elders, gathered at the LORD's house to hear the book and stood to join the covenant. Huldah lived there in the second quarter.

l: Shaphan, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Shaphan the son of Azaliah was sent by Josiah, with Maaseiah and Joah, to repair the house of the LORD. He received the found book from Hilkiah, reported on the work to the king, and read the book to him. He was also among those sent to inquire of the LORD.

l: Hilkiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Hilkiah the high priest received the money for the repairs and, while it was being brought out, found the book of the LORD's law given by Moses. He gave it to Shaphan. He was commanded by Josiah to go inquire of the LORD and went with others to Huldah.

l: Huldah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum and keeper of the wardrobe, lived in Jerusalem's second quarter. When consulted by Hilkiah and the king's men, she delivered the LORD's message of coming judgment on the place and of peace for Josiah in his lifetime.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: The house of the LORD was repaired in Josiah's eighteenth year with money gathered by the Levites from Manasseh, Ephraim, Israel's remnant, Judah, Benjamin, and Jerusalem. Workmen, carpenters, and builders bought cut stone and timber to mend buildings the kings of Judah had destroyed. The book of the law was found there, and Josiah read the covenant there to the people.

l: book of the law, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: The book of the LORD's law given by Moses was found by Hilkiah in the LORD's house and passed to Shaphan, who read it to Josiah. Its words caused the king to tear his clothes and seek the LORD's word. Josiah later read it as the book of the covenant to all the people.

l: idolatrous objects and altars, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: The altars of the Baals, incense altars, Asherah poles, engraved images, and molten images were broken down, cut down, and ground to dust under Josiah's direction. The dust was scattered on the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. This extended throughout Israel, and Josiah took away all abominations from the lands of the children of Israel.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: In his eighteenth year Josiah sent Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah to repair the house of the LORD with money delivered through Hilkiah to the overseers and workmen. The men worked faithfully under Levite overseers Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. During this work the book of the law was found.

l: purge of idolatry, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Beginning in his twelfth year, Josiah purged Judah and Jerusalem of high places and images, burned the bones of the priests on their altars, and extended the work to the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali. He then returned to Jerusalem. The work preceded the temple repair and the finding of the book.

l: covenant renewal, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 34
s: Josiah gathered the elders and all the people, great and small, to the LORD's house and read them the book of the covenant. Standing in his place, he covenanted to walk after the LORD and keep his commandments with all his heart and soul. He made those in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand, and they acted according to the covenant.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Josiah keeps a great Passover in Jerusalem, setting the priests and Levites in their offices and providing thousands of lambs, young goats, and bulls from his own substance, with his princes and the chiefs of the Levites also giving generously. The priests sprinkle the blood and the Levites skin the animals and prepare the offerings, so that the singers and gatekeepers need not leave their posts. The text says no Passover like it had been kept since the days of Samuel, and it took place in Josiah's eighteenth year. Afterward Neco king of Egypt goes up to fight at Carchemish, warns Josiah that God has commanded him, and Josiah refuses to listen and fights him in the valley of Megiddo. Archers wound Josiah, he is taken to Jerusalem and dies, and Judah, Jerusalem, and Jeremiah mourn him.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Josiah keeps a Passover in Jerusalem, sets the priests in their offices, instructs the Levites, and supplies thousands of lambs, young goats, and bulls from his own substance. Later he disregards Neco's warning, which came from the mouth of God, disguises himself, and fights at Megiddo, where archers wound him. He dies in Jerusalem, is buried in the tombs of his fathers, and is mourned by all Judah and Jerusalem and by Jeremiah.

l: Passover (Josiah's Passover), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: The Passover is killed on the fourteenth day of the first month in Jerusalem and followed by the feast of unleavened bread for seven days. The animals are provided by the king, his princes, and the chiefs of the Levites, and the service is carried out according to the king's commandment. The text says no Passover like it had been kept in Israel since Samuel the prophet, and it took place in Josiah's eighteenth year.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: The Passover and the burnt offerings are offered to the LORD according to the word given by Moses and the book of Moses. Neco says that God has commanded him to make haste and that God is with him. The text says Neco's words came from the mouth of God, and Josiah did not listen to them.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Josiah sets the priests in their offices and encourages them in the service of the LORD's house. At the Passover they sprinkle the blood received from the Levites' hands and are busy offering the burnt offerings and the fat until night. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, rulers of God's house, give them two thousand six hundred small livestock and three hundred head of cattle for the Passover offerings.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Josiah tells the Levites, who taught all Israel, to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built, to prepare by their divisions, and to kill the Passover lamb. They skin the animals, roast and boil the offerings, and carry them quickly to the people. They also prepare for themselves, for the priests, and for the singers and gatekeepers, and their chiefs Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad give five thousand small livestock and five hundred head of cattle.

l: king of Egypt (Neco), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Neco king of Egypt goes up to fight against Carchemish by the Euphrates. He sends ambassadors telling Josiah that he comes not against him but against another house, and that God has commanded him to make haste and warns Josiah to stop opposing God. Josiah does not turn back and fights him at Megiddo.

l: battle at Megiddo (Josiah's death), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 35
s: Josiah, disguised, comes to fight Neco in the valley of Megiddo, where archers shoot him and he says he is seriously wounded. His servants move him to his second chariot and bring him to Jerusalem, where he dies and is buried in his fathers' tombs. All Judah and Jerusalem mourn him, and Jeremiah and the singing men and women lament him in laments that became an ordinance in Israel.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Chapter 36 recounts the last kings of Judah. The people make Jehoahaz king, but the king of Egypt removes him after three months, fines the land, and installs Eliakim, renamed Jehoiakim, while Neco carries Joahaz to Egypt. Jehoiakim does evil and Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon binds him and takes vessels of the LORD's house to Babylon; his son Jehoiachin reigns briefly and is also taken to Babylon, and Zedekiah is made king. Zedekiah, the priests, and the people rebel and pollute the LORD's house, mock the prophets, and so the Chaldeans burn the temple and Jerusalem and carry survivors to Babylon for seventy years. In Cyrus of Persia's first year, the LORD stirs him to proclaim that he is to build the LORD a house in Jerusalem and that God's people may go up.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Jerusalem is where Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah reign in turn. Its wall is broken down and its palaces burned by the Chaldeans. Cyrus later commands that a house for the LORD be built there.

l: Jehoiakim, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Jehoiakim, formerly Eliakim, is made king by the king of Egypt in place of his brother Joahaz and renamed. He reigns eleven years from age twenty-five and does evil in the LORD's sight. Nebuchadnezzar binds him in fetters to carry him to Babylon, and his son Jehoiachin succeeds him.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon comes up against Jehoiakim, binds him, and takes vessels of the LORD's house to his temple in Babylon. He later brings Jehoiachin to Babylon and makes Zedekiah king, who rebels against him despite having sworn by God.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Babylon receives Jehoiakim's captive party, vessels of the LORD's house, and Jehoiachin. All the vessels, treasures, and surviving people of Judah are brought there, where the survivors serve Nebuchadnezzar and his sons until Persia's reign.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: The LORD sent messengers early and often to his people out of compassion, but they mocked them until his wrath arose and there was no remedy. He brought the Chaldeans against them, and fulfilled his word by Jeremiah through seventy years of Sabbath desolation. He then stirred up Cyrus's spirit to proclaim the rebuilding of his house.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Vessels of the LORD's house are carried off to Babylon in stages under Nebuchadnezzar. The priests and people pollute it, and finally the Chaldeans slay young men in the sanctuary, take all its vessels and treasures, and burn it. Cyrus is later commanded to build a house for the LORD in Jerusalem.

l: Zedekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Zedekiah is made king by Nebuchadnezzar in place of his brother Jehoiachin and reigns eleven years from age twenty-one. He does evil, does not humble himself before Jeremiah, rebels against Nebuchadnezzar despite his oath by God, and hardens his heart against turning to the LORD.

l: Jeremiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Jeremiah the prophet speaks from the LORD's mouth, but Zedekiah does not humble himself before him. His word is fulfilled in the seventy years of the land's Sabbath desolation, and again when the LORD stirs up Cyrus.

l: chiefs of the priests and the people, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: The chiefs of the priests and the people trespass greatly, following the abominations of the nations and polluting the LORD's house. They mock God's messengers, despise his words, and scoff at his prophets until his wrath rises beyond remedy.

l: destruction of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: The king of the Chaldeans kills young and old, even in the sanctuary, and takes all vessels and treasures to Babylon. His forces burn God's house, break down Jerusalem's wall, burn its palaces, and destroy its valuable vessels. Survivors are carried to Babylon, and the land lies desolate to fulfill seventy years.

l: Cyrus, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: Cyrus king of Persia, in his first year, has his spirit stirred up by the LORD to fulfill Jeremiah's word. He makes a proclamation throughout his kingdom, in speech and in writing, saying the LORD has given him all the kingdoms of the earth.

l: proclamation of Cyrus, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 36
s: The proclamation is made orally and in writing throughout Cyrus's kingdom. It states that the LORD, the God of heaven, commanded Cyrus to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judah, and invites any of his people to go up, with the LORD's presence.

l: The Book of Haggai, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: In the second year of King Darius, the LORD of Armies sends a message through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor of Judah and Joshua the high priest. The people claim it is not yet time to build the LORD's house, but the LORD asks why they dwell in paneled houses while his house lies waste. He tells them to consider their ways, pointing out that their labor yields little because of drought and loss, which he attributes to their neglect of his house. He commands them to bring wood and build, promising to take pleasure in it and be glorified. Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant obey, the LORD affirms 'I am with you,' stirs their spirits, and they begin work on the house on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month.

l: the LORD of Armies, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: The LORD of Armies speaks through Haggai, rebuking the people for living in paneled houses while his house lies waste, and telling them to consider their ways. He explains that he caused their meager harvests and called for drought because of their neglect, and commands them to build the house. He then declares 'I am with you' and stirs up the spirits of the leaders and the remnant to begin work.

l: Haggai, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: Haggai the prophet receives the LORD's word and delivers it to Zerubbabel and Joshua. He is called the LORD's messenger, and he speaks the message 'I am with you' to the people. The people obey his words as the LORD had sent him.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, is addressed by the LORD's word through Haggai. He obeys the LORD's voice together with Joshua and the remnant, and the LORD stirs up his spirit so that he comes and works on the LORD's house.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: Joshua, the high priest, is addressed alongside Zerubbabel in the LORD's message through Haggai. He obeys the LORD's voice, has his spirit stirred by the LORD, and joins the work on the house.

l: the temple (the LORD’s house), The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: The LORD's house is described as lying waste while the people live in paneled houses, and the people say the time has not come to build it. The LORD commands that wood be brought and the house built, saying he will take pleasure in it and be glorified. Work on it begins on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius.

l: remnant of the people, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 1
s: The remnant of the people, along with Zerubbabel and Joshua, obey the LORD's voice and the words of Haggai, and they fear the LORD. The LORD stirs up their spirit, and they come and work on the house of the LORD of Armies.

l: The Book of Haggai, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: In Haggai chapter 2, the LORD's word comes through Haggai the prophet on three occasions in the seventh and ninth months of Darius's second year. First he tells Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and the remnant to be strong and work on the seemingly humble house because the LORD is with them, promising to shake the heavens, earth, and nations, fill the house with glory, and make its latter glory greater than the former. Then Haggai asks the priests about holiness and uncleanness, using their answers to show that the people and their offerings are unclean, and recalls how blight, mildew, and hail reduced their harvests before the temple's foundation was laid. The LORD promises to bless them from that day. Finally the LORD tells Zerubbabel that he will shake the heavens and earth, overthrow the kingdoms and their chariots, and make Zerubbabel his chosen signet ring.

l: the LORD of Armies, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: The LORD of Armies speaks through Haggai, urging the leaders and people to be strong and work because he is with them. He promises to shake the nations, fill the house with glory, give peace, and bless the people from the day of the foundation onward. He declares that the silver and gold are his, and that he has chosen Zerubbabel as his signet ring.

l: Haggai, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: Haggai the prophet delivers the LORD's word to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant on the twenty-first day of the seventh month and twice on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. He questions the priests about the law of holiness and uncleanness and applies their answers to declare the people and their offerings unclean.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel and governor of Judah, is told to be strong and work, since the LORD is with him. In the second word he is promised that when the LORD overthrows the kingdoms, he will be taken as the LORD's servant and made like a signet ring because the LORD has chosen him.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, is addressed along with Zerubbabel and the remnant and is told to be strong and work because the LORD is with him.

l: remnant of the people, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: The remnant of the people is addressed with Zerubbabel and Joshua and told to be strong, work, and not be afraid. Haggai describes the people as unclean along with the work of their hands, and notes that they suffered poor harvests from blight, mildew, and hail without turning to the LORD. The LORD promises to bless them from that day.

l: the shaking of heavens and earth, The Book of Haggai, Chapter 2
s: The LORD announces that in a little while he will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land, and all nations, so that their treasure comes to the house. He repeats the promise to Zerubbabel, adding that he will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, destroy the strength of the nations, and bring down chariots and horsemen, who will fall by the sword of one another.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: In the second year of Darius, the LORD's word comes to the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah and son of Iddo, first calling the people to return to him and not be like their fathers, who ignored the former prophets yet later admitted the LORD had dealt with them as their ways deserved. On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Zechariah has a night vision of a man on a red horse among myrtle trees with red, brown, and white horses that have walked through the earth and found it at rest. The LORD's angel asks how long the LORD will withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah after seventy years, and the LORD answers with kind words. Through the interpreting angel the LORD proclaims that he is jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, angry with the nations at ease, and has returned to Jerusalem with mercy so that his house will be built and his cities will overflow with prosperity. Zechariah then sees four horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem, and four craftsmen who come to terrify them and cast down the horns of the nations.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD of Armies calls the people to return to him so that he will return to them, and recalls that he was very displeased with their fathers. He declares that he is jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, angry with the nations that are at ease, and that he has returned to Jerusalem with mercy so his house will be built and his cities will prosper.

l: Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: Zechariah, the prophet son of Berechiah and son of Iddo, receives the LORD's word in the eighth month of Darius's second year and again on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month. He sees a night vision of a man on a red horse, horses, four horns, and four craftsmen, and asks the angel who talked with him to explain them.

l: fathers (Zechariah's audience's fathers), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The fathers were the object of the LORD's great displeasure, and they did not hear or listen when the former prophets urged them to turn from evil ways. The LORD's words and decrees overtook them, and they then repented, saying the LORD had dealt with them according to their ways and practices.

l: man on the red horse (in Zechariah's vision), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The man on a red horse stands among the myrtle trees in a ravine, with red, brown, and white horses behind him. He explains that the horses are those the LORD has sent to go back and forth through the earth.

l: angel who talked with me (Zechariah's interpreting angel), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: This angel tells Zechariah he will show him what the horses are, and he is answered by the LORD with kind and comforting words. He instructs Zechariah to proclaim the LORD's jealousy for Jerusalem and Zion, and explains the four horns and the four craftsmen.

l: the LORD's angel, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD's angel stands among the myrtle trees and receives the report that all the earth is at rest and in peace. He then asks the LORD of Armies how long he will withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah after seventy years of indignation.

l: horses (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The red, brown, and white horses stand behind the man among the myrtle trees. They are the ones the LORD sent to go back and forth through the earth, and they report that all the earth is at rest and in peace.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem has been under the LORD's indignation for seventy years, and the LORD's angel pleads for mercy for it. The LORD says he is jealous for it, has returned to it with mercy, that his house will be built in it with a line stretched over it, and that he will again choose it.

l: Zion, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he is jealous for Zion with a great jealousy. He promises that he will again comfort Zion.

l: Judah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: Judah and its cities have been under the LORD's indignation for seventy years. Judah was scattered by the horns so that no man lifted up his head, and the craftsmen come to cast down the horns of the nations that lifted up their horn against the land of Judah.

l: nations, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The nations are at ease, and the LORD is very angry with them because he was only a little displeased but they added to the calamity. The horns of the nations that lifted up their horn against Judah are to be cast down.

l: four horns (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: Zechariah sees four horns, which the angel says have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. They represent the horns of the nations that lifted up their horn against the land of Judah to scatter it.

l: four craftsmen (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD shows Zechariah four craftsmen. They have come to terrify the horns and cast down the horns of the nations that scattered Judah.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: The narrator sees a man with a measuring line who is going to measure Jerusalem's width and length. The angel who talked with the narrator goes out, and another angel meets him and sends a message for the young man: Jerusalem will be inhabited as unwalled villages because of its many people and livestock, with the LORD as a wall of fire around it and the glory within it. The LORD calls those in the land of the north and those dwelling with the daughter of Babylon to flee, and says he will shake his hand over the nations that plundered Zion's people so they become plunder for their former servants. Zion is told to sing and rejoice because the LORD comes to dwell within her, many nations will join themselves to him, and he will again choose Jerusalem and inherit Judah. All flesh is told to be silent because the LORD has roused himself from his holy habitation.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem is about to be measured for its width and length by a man with a measuring line. It is told that it will be inhabited as villages without walls because of the multitude of men and livestock in it, with the LORD as a wall of fire around it and the glory in its middle. The LORD will again choose Jerusalem.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD promises to be a wall of fire around Jerusalem and the glory in her middle, and calls his people to flee the north and Babylon. He has sent a messenger to the nations that plundered his people, will shake his hand over them, and declares he will dwell within Zion and among his people. He will inherit Judah in the holy land, again choose Jerusalem, and has roused himself from his holy habitation.

l: man with a measuring line, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: The man with a measuring line appears to the narrator holding it in his hand. Asked where he is going, he answers that he is going to measure Jerusalem to see its width and length.

l: angel who talked with me (Zechariah's interpreting angel), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: The angel who talked with the narrator goes out, and another angel goes out to meet him. The other angel then tells him to run and speak to the young man with the message about Jerusalem.

l: Zion, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: Zion is told to escape from those who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. The daughter of Zion is told to sing and rejoice because the LORD is coming to dwell within her. Those who touch Zion's people are said to touch the apple of his eye.

l: many nations, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: Many nations are said to join themselves to the LORD in that day and to become his people. A separate group of nations that plundered the LORD's people will themselves become plunder to those who served them, when the LORD shakes his hand over them.

l: people of Jerusalem (Jerusalem's inhabitants), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 2
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem, men and livestock, are numerous enough that the city will be inhabited as villages without walls. They are protected by the LORD as a wall of fire. Those in the north and with Babylon are called to flee and come, having been spread abroad like the four winds of the sky.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: In a vision, Joshua the high priest stands before the LORD's angel while Satan stands at his right hand as adversary. The LORD rebukes Satan and calls Joshua a burning stick plucked from the fire. Joshua's filthy garments are removed, his iniquity is declared passed from him, and he is clothed with rich clothing and given a clean turban. The LORD's angel then charges Joshua that if he walks in the LORD's ways and follows his instructions, he will judge and keep the LORD's house and courts and have access among those standing by. The LORD of Armies announces that he will bring out his servant, the Branch, engrave an inscription on a stone with seven eyes, remove the land's iniquity in one day, and that people will then invite neighbors under vine and fig tree.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: Joshua stands before the LORD's angel in filthy garments while Satan opposes him, and is called a burning stick plucked out of the fire. His garments are exchanged for rich clothing and a clean turban, and he is told that if he walks in the LORD's ways and follows his instructions he will judge and keep the LORD's house and courts. He and his fellows are described as men who are a sign.

l: the LORD's angel, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD's angel presides over the scene in which Joshua stands before him, and stands by as Joshua is given a clean turban and clothed. He solemnly assures Joshua and delivers the LORD of Armies' conditional promise.

l: Satan, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: Satan stands at Joshua's right hand to be his adversary. The LORD rebukes him twice, and he is not recorded as saying anything.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD rebukes Satan, citing his choice of Jerusalem, and describes Joshua as a burning stick plucked from the fire. As the LORD of Armies, he promises access and authority to Joshua on condition of obedience, says he will bring out his servant the Branch, will engrave an inscription on the stone, and will remove the land's iniquity in one day.

l: filthy garments (Joshua's garments), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: Joshua is clothed in filthy garments as he stands before the angel. Those standing before the speaker are told to take them off him, and he is clothed with rich clothing instead.

l: Joshua's iniquity, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker declares that he has caused Joshua's iniquity to pass from him, which is paired with the removal of the filthy garments. The LORD also says he will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.

l: the Branch, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 3
s: The Branch is named as the LORD's servant whom the LORD says he will bring out. Joshua and his fellows are described as men who are a sign in connection with this promise.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 4
s: The angel who talked with the narrator wakes him and asks what he sees. The narrator describes a golden lamp stand with a bowl, seven lamps, seven pipes to each lamp, and two olive trees beside it. He does not understand the vision, so the angel gives the LORD's word to Zerubbabel: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit." The LORD of Armies promises that Zerubbabel, who laid the foundation of the house, will also finish it, and that the great mountain before him will become a plain. The angel explains that the seven are the LORD's eyes running through the whole earth, and that the two olive trees are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD of Armies gives a word to Zerubbabel: the work is accomplished "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit." He promises that Zerubbabel's hands will finish the house, and that this will show the narrator that he has been sent. The seven are said to be the LORD's eyes running through the whole earth.

l: Zerubbabel, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 4
s: Zerubbabel receives the LORD's word that the work depends on the Spirit, not might or power. The great mountain becomes a plain before him, and he will bring out the capstone amid shouts of "Grace, grace, to it!" His hands laid the foundation of the house and will also finish it, and he will hold the plumb line.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The narrator sees a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten wide, which an unnamed speaker explains is a curse going out over the whole land against thieves and those who swear falsely. The LORD of Armies declares he will send it into the houses of such people, where it will remain and destroy the house with its timber and stones. The angel who talked with the narrator then shows him an ephah basket appearing, with a lead cover lifted to reveal a woman sitting inside, whom the angel names Wickedness. The angel throws her back into the basket and weights its mouth with lead. Two winged women, with the wind in their wings like those of a stork, lift the basket between earth and sky and carry it to the land of Shinar, where a house will be built for her and she will be set in her own place.

l: flying scroll, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The narrator sees the flying scroll, which measures twenty cubits by ten cubits. It is identified as the curse going out over the surface of the whole land.

l: curse (the flying scroll's curse), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The curse goes out over the whole land, cutting off thieves according to one side and false swearers according to the other. The LORD says it will enter the houses of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by his name, and remain there until it destroys the house with its timber and stones.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD of Armies declares that he will cause the curse to go out. He says it will enter the houses of the thief and of him who swears falsely by his name and destroy them.

l: angel who talked with me (Zechariah's interpreting angel), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The angel asks the narrator what he sees, tells him to look at the appearing ephah basket, and explains what it is. He identifies the woman as Wickedness, throws her into the basket, and throws the lead weight on its mouth. He also tells the narrator that the basket is being carried to Shinar.

l: Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The narrator lifts his eyes and sees the flying scroll, describing its dimensions when asked. He then sees the ephah basket, the woman inside it, and the two winged women lifting it. He asks the angel where it is being carried.

l: ephah basket, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The ephah basket appears and is described as the appearance of them in all the land. It has a lead cover weighing a talent, and a woman sits in it. After she is thrown in and the cover is placed on its mouth, two women lift it between earth and sky to carry it to Shinar.

l: Wickedness, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: The angel names the woman sitting in the ephah basket as Wickedness. He throws her down into the basket and weights its mouth with lead. She is carried off to Shinar, where a house will be built for her and she will be set in her own place.

l: two women (who carry the ephah basket), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: Two women appear with the wind in their wings, which are like the wings of a stork. They lift up the ephah basket between earth and sky to carry it away.

l: Shinar, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 5
s: Shinar is named as the destination of the ephah basket. A house is to be built there for Wickedness, and when it is prepared she will be set in her own place.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: In a vision, the narrator sees four chariots, drawn by red, black, white, and dappled horses, come out from between two bronze mountains. The angel who talks with him explains that they are the four winds of the sky, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth, and they walk back and forth through the earth, with those going north quieting the LORD's spirit there. The LORD's word then tells the narrator to take silver and gold from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, who have come from Babylon to the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah, and make crowns for Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Joshua is to be told of the man named the Branch, who will grow up out of his place, build the LORD's temple, bear glory, and rule as a priest on his throne, and the crowns will be a memorial in the temple. Those far off will come and build, and the promise depends on diligent obedience to the LORD's voice.

l: four chariots, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains, pulled by red, black, white, and dappled horses, all of them powerful. They are identified as the four winds of the sky, and they go out to the north and south countries and walk back and forth through the earth.

l: angel who talked with me (Zechariah's interpreting angel), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The angel answers the narrator's question about the chariots, explaining that they are the four winds of the sky that go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. He also tells the narrator that those who go toward the north country have quieted his spirit there.

l: narrator (Zechariah), The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The narrator lifts up his eyes and sees four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains, and asks the angel what they are. He then receives the LORD's word instructing him to take silver and gold from the exiles, make crowns, set them on Joshua's head, and deliver the message about the Branch.

l: four winds of the sky, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The four chariots are identified as the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. They are told to go around and through the earth and do so, and those going toward the north country are said to have quieted the LORD's spirit in the north.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD is the Lord of all the earth, before whom the four winds stand before going out, and he sends them to walk through the earth. His word commands the making of crowns for Joshua and promises the Branch who will build his temple, and he says that far-off people will come and build if the people diligently obey his voice.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: Joshua, the high priest, is to have crowns of silver and gold set on his head, taken from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah. He is to be told the message about the man called the Branch.

l: crowns, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The crowns are to be made from silver and gold taken from the exiles who came from Babylon, and are to be set on the head of Joshua the high priest. They are afterwards to belong to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen the son of Zephaniah as a memorial in the LORD's temple.

l: the Branch, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 6
s: The Branch is a man who will grow up out of his place and build the LORD's temple. He will bear the glory, sit and rule on his throne, and be a priest on his throne, with the counsel of peace between them both.

l: The Book of Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 7
